description: We are a team passionate about coding, game development, web development, and space exploration. We combine creativity, storytelling, and data visualization to build interactive, educational experiences. Inspired by Mars and human exploration, we aim to use technology and NASA's open data to make complex scientific concepts engaging, promote resource awareness, and inspire curiosity about the universe.
summary: Mars Base: Sol 30 is a free browser game that teaches children aged 7–12 the real trade-offs of running a Mars outpost. Players manage a small base for 30 Martian days (sols), choosing one job each sol: research, recycling air and water, growing food, cleaning solar panels, or resting. Power, life support, food, crew health, research and radiation exposure are linked, so every choice has a cost. Events such as a dust storm, a water leak, a crop blight and a solar flare force hard decisions, and Earth’s replies arrive late, so players must decide for themselves. The solar flare event is built from a real NASA DONKI space weather record, clearly separated from simulated game values. After each choice, Buddy the robot explains the science. A final report scores crew safety, supplies and research and shows why a mission failed, encouraging replay with a new strategy. The game aims to show young learners that space exploration is about careful planning, not luck, and to make NASA science feel approachable. It runs in any modern browser with no account or install, includes saved NASA data as a fallback, and works on tablets and phones in landscape. Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
details:
The player is the commander of a Mars base and plays 30 sols. Each sol, they tap a part of the base to do one job: the microscope for research, the recycler for air and water, the solar panels to clear dust, the sleeping pod to rest, and the control console to plant a greenhouse crop. Every job costs something. Research uses power, recycling uses power, and crops take five sols to grow, so players must plan ahead.

Six meters track the base: power, life support, food, crew health, research and radiation dose. Each sol, the crew uses air, water and food, and the base spends energy on heating and pumps. If power hits zero, life support drops faster. If life support or food runs out, the crew gets hurt.

Five story events break the routine: a dust storm that cuts solar power, a solar flare, a water leak, a crop blight and an ice discovery. Each has two choices, such as sheltering from a flare, which costs research time, or working outside, which gives more science but adds simulated radiation. Players can ask Earth for advice, but the reply takes two sols, so they must decide first.

After every action, Buddy the robot shows the changes and explains the science, for example why recycling and power are linked. At the end, a report gives star ratings and explains why a mission failed, such as running out of food, with a tip to try a different strategy.

NASA data

The solar flare event uses a real record from NASA’s DONKI space weather database: an X1.0 flare from Active Region 13664 on 8 May 2024, with its record ID and a link to NASA. The event card also cites the radiation that Curiosity measured on Mars during a solar storm in May 2024, as reported by Space.com. The game keeps real data and simulated values in two separate boxes. The radiation numbers used in play are labelled as game units, not Mars measurements. The deployed version also tries to load a recent strong flare live from the NASA DONKI API. If that fails, it uses the saved record, so the game always works.

Benefits and intended impact

Children learn that every choice on Mars has a trade-off. Saving power can hurt life support, and gathering more science can mean accepting radiation risk. They also learn why space weather matters to astronauts. The game needs no account, no install and no cost, so a classroom, library or home can use it right away. We hope it makes space science feel like a decision children can make, which encourages curiosity about careers in space and science.

Tools and technology

  • HTML5, CSS3 (grid layout) and plain JavaScript, with a custom turn-based game engine and no backend
  • NASA DONKI API through api.nasa.gov, with a local JSON-style fallback
  • Browser local storage for the best score
  • Google Fonts (Unbounded and Fredoka)
  • Python with Pillow and SciPy to prepare the artwork
  • A free metal texture by Magda Ehlers from Pexels
  • Claude, an AI assistant, helped write and test the code and text. I directed the design and checked the content.
  • Planned hosting: Vercel. No special hardware is needed.

Creativity

The base is a cutaway picture the player taps, so choosing a job feels like walking through a real habitat instead of picking from a menu. Buddy the robot reacts with different facts. The astronaut walks to each part of the base and waves. Earth’s late replies turn a real space-communication problem into a game choice. Clear labels separate NASA facts from game numbers, which models honest science for children.

Factors we considered

  • Age and language: short sentences, simple words, and emoji icons for each meter
  • Scientific honesty: real NASA data is separate from simulated values, with sources and a not-official-NASA note
  • Accessibility: large tap targets, readable colours, keyboard focus outlines, reduced-motion support, and text labels with every number
  • Reliability: works offline with saved data, and the game never crashes if the NASA API is down
  • Devices: works on computers and tablets, and phones in landscape, with a prompt to turn the phone sideways
  • Replayability: different choices give different endings
  • Safety and licensing: no accounts, no personal data, and credited image sources
